newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Banks ready aid as Swiss humanitarian fund falters.
newsitem.headline: Banks ready aid as Swiss humanitarian fund falters.

text.p: Big Swiss banks are ready to throw their weight behind a proposed humanitarian foundation assisting victims of poverty and disasters amid signs that public opinion is turning against the scheme, a top banker said on Wednesday.

The banker, who asked not to be named, said banks would help fund a public relations drive for the seven billion Swiss franc foundation, which the Berne government hopes will clear the air of allegations Switzerland coolly profited from World War Two.

But an opinion poll in the L'Illustre magazine found support for the plan, announced by President Arnold Koller in March, was starting to wane amid sniping from right-wing politicians who say the Swiss are caving in to foreign blackmail.

The survey of 571 Swiss this month showed 43 percent of respondents oppose the plan and 40 percent favour the idea of selling off part of Switzerland's official gold reserves to help victims of poverty and catastrophes in Switzerland and abroad.
If they were voting this Sunday, 11 percent were unsure how to cast their ballot and six percent said it depended on how the foundation was organised, said the survey.
This was a far cry from the majorities of 50 to 70 percent that backed the idea when Koller first proposed it.

Next year's referendum is shaping up as a watershed event in Swiss domestic politics and foreign relations, and top banks want to help assure a victory that will help restore Switzerland's battered image around the world.

"Most of us are realising that the government has decided on something and we now have to back it up. To shoot it down would be very, very short-sighted," the senior official at one of the country's leading banks told reporters.

"I think when we move closer to the date when the vote will take place we will rally together and put some money at the disposal of trade organisations and so on who will lead the campaign forward," he added.
"If I were a betting man I would say it is going to happen, but it is going to take a lot of work."
Proponents of the fund say it would show Swiss gratitude that the tiny neutral land escaped the horrors of World War Two although surrounded by the Axis.

Opponents call it an ill-considered sell-off of national treasure in the face of pressure from foreign critics like U.S. Senator Alfonse D'Amato and Jewish groups who accuse Swiss banks of hoarding the unclaimed assets of Holocaust victims.
The banker said his optimism was tinged by reservations that the Swiss could vote down the plan as a way to thumb their nose at foreign critics and assert Swiss sovereignty.

"If the Swiss people are pushed around too much by political considerations -- and let's face it, for the politicians it's a no-lose situation -- then at some point in time there could be a backlash," he said, citing the decline in opinion polls.
"I was surprised it is still as high as 40 percent, which to me is a very positive sign," he added.

To help make the scheme more politically palatable, Jewish groups have already suggested dropping any reference to Holocaust victims as recipients of largesse from the foundation and paying them instead from a separate memorial fund.
Swiss banks, other private businesses and the Swiss National Bank are putting up 265 million francs in that fund to alleviate the suffering of needy Holocaust survivors and their families.

The foundation plan announced by Koller, on the other hand, calls for revaluing official gold reserves -- now on the central bank's books at less than a third of their market value -- by 14 billion francs, half of which would finance the fund.

Gradually selling seven billion worth of gold and investing the proceeds in securities would generate around 350 million Swiss francs a year to distribute to victims of poverty, human rights abuses and disasters in Switzerland and abroad.
